title: Build exporter shim for span enrichment and dynamic backend routing
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
Create a vendor-agnostic exporter shim that sits between our OpenTelemetry ingestion layer and downstream tracing backends. The shim will: enrich spans with routing and tenant context, carry sampling metadata for correct downstream retention, and enable dynamic routing/failover across multiple backends (e.g., vendor A, vendor B, and our internal long-term storage) via feature flags.

Motivation:
We currently have brittle wiring for exporting trace data to third-party backends. Customers and platform teams need: (1) consistent tenant and sampling metadata in exported spans for multi-tenant analytics, (2) the ability to move traffic between tracing backends without SDK-level changes, and (3) a low-risk canary/fallback flow for backend upgrades. Building a lightweight shim reduces coupling in the ingestion path and centralizes enrichment and routing logic.

Goals / Acceptance criteria:
- Shim accepts OTLP protobuf/span batches and can emit to multiple exporters (HTTP/Thrift/OTLP) configured per-tenant or per-route.
- Each exported span contains a standardized set of enrichment fields: tenant_id, tenant_tier, sampling_decision_reason, original_sampling_rate, and route_metadata.
- Shim preserves trace_id/span_id and sampling bits so downstream systems can correlate with logs/metrics and honor sampling decisions.
- Dynamic routing toggles via LaunchDarkly (or equivalent) flags and can switch a tenant from backend X->Y with zero client SDK changes.
- Provide a fallback chain: primary -> secondary -> local-buffer -> drop, with metrics exposed for each step.
- End-to-end latency added by the shim at p95 must be <2ms for in-region traffic at 1x baseline load, and CPU/memory overhead must be documented in README.
- Integration tests that run an OTLP span through the shim and validate enrichment, routing, and fallback behavior.

Design notes / Implementation approach:
1) Interface: shim exposes an OTLP gRPC/HTTP endpoint compatible with our existing collector configuration. It will accept both proto and JSON formats.
2) Enrichment pipeline: on receipt, attach tenant context from request headers (x-redwood-tenant, x-tenant-tier) and sampling metadata from the collector sampler. If headers missing, consult tenant resolution cache populated by our tenant-mapper service.
3) Exporter adapters: implement adapter interfaces for OTLP/HTTP/Thrift backends. Each adapter serializes spans according to backend expectations and can add backend-specific attributes.
4) Routing & flags: route decisions are evaluated in this order: explicit per-tenant config -> percentage rollout (feature flag) -> default backend. Support percentage-based canaries.
5) Buffering: small local in-memory ring buffer with bounded size per-tenant for transient backend failures; flush policy exponential backoff and metric emission when buffers saturate.
6) Observability: emit metrics for inbound spans, enrichment failures, routing decision counts, export success/failures, buffer saturation, and export latency histograms. Trace the shim itself with a light-weight internal span.
7) Tests: unit tests for enrichment logic, adapter mocks for exporters, chaos tests to validate fallback behavior, and performance benchmarks.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (canary): deploy shim in a single region for internal telemetry only, with per-tenant routing flags set to keep most traffic on existing path. Monitor metrics for 48h.
- Stage 2 (selected customers): enable for a small set of customers with opt-in, verify enrichment fields land in downstream UIs and dashboards.
- Stage 3 (global): flip default routing over to new shim, keep fallback chain active for 2 weeks before removing extra buffering.

Backwards compatibility and migration:
- We will not alter client SDKs. The shim must preserve sampling bits and trace identifiers. Existing dashboards that rely on specific backend attributes must be validated against the enrichment fields; provide a translation map for common attributes.

Security considerations:
- Ensure any tenant_id enrichment is added server-side and cannot be spoofed from untrusted upstreams. Validate headers against authentication context.
- Transport TLS for all backend exporters; support mTLS if configured by enterprise customers.

Risks & mitigation:
- Risk: Added latency under high load. Mitigation: benchmark early, implement adaptive batching and limit enrichment work to a fast-path.
- Risk: Incomplete tenant mapping for some span sources. Mitigation: default to tenant_resolver fallback and emit diagnostic metrics for manual reconciliation.

Documentation & operational runbook:
- README with config examples, adapter templates, and observed resource usage.
- Runbook entries: how to add a new backend adapter, steps to flip routing flags, and emergency rollback.
